title: Use Tone And Say What I Learnt
objective: Continue the drawing activity, try ways to make light and dark tones, and explain what you learnt.

blocks.text: BUILD · Art · Week 1. Trinity Arts Award Explore. Use Tone And Say What I Learnt.
Objective: Continue the drawing activity, try ways to make light and dark tones, and explain what you learnt.
Success evidence: a selected tone drawing, a record of taking part, and your own learning from the drawing activity.
Theme: Making and Sharing. Make choices about the art. You may keep your private life private.
40 minutes. Use the materials prepared on your table.

This deck contributes to Explore Part A, Take part: at least two arts activities and identification of what the pupil learnt. In this strand, drawing is activity one and paper sculpture is activity two. Two lessons in drawing are still one arts activity. Do not claim Part A complete until both activities and learning are evidenced. Award requirements come only from tools/artsaward/SPEC.json, Explore. Overall Pass allows ONE Attempted. Any Not Attempted = Below Pass. The whole Explore portfolio has a 10-file cap. Its three assessment areas are art form knowledge and understanding, creativity, and communication. Only an adviser trained at Explore may assess; delivery must be through a validated centre. Confirm both locally; neither is asserted as already confirmed. Core, Extend and Challenge are support options within Explore, not different awards. They retain participation and the pupil’s own learning. Scribe exact pupil words when needed, read them back and accept correction; do not compose or upgrade their account. Keep evidence in the cumulative Explore-A file with its actual file name plus page, slide or timecode. The proposed four part-files are a filing option, not a mandatory award format. Suggested sample counts are teaching scaffolds, not extra award quotas. This is secondary SEMH teaching in the BUILD reading band. Discuss artistic choices; do not require private-life disclosure. These sessions support the wider programme; they do not claim to supply all 25 guided and 10 independent hours.

Prepare plain paper, drawing pencils, optional grips and the pupil’s line drawing where available. A missing drawing does not stop new participation: supply fresh paper and let the pupil make a simple shape. On the board draw three labelled equal boxes: A left white, B shaded lightly, C made darker with further gentle layers. Provide a separate pair of equal shapes, one with a dark edge against a pale area and one with similar tones together. Make these models live; no external artwork is needed. Put the four sorting statements from We Do on the board. Every learner needs a practice area and a final drawing area. Check comfortable tools and keep a spare sheet to protect the table. Do not introduce numerical improvement targets or call tone a second arts activity.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve
stages.data-ta1: Retrieve existing work without making its absence a punishment. Check grip and reach; offer fresh paper rather than suggesting a pupil has already completed a missing task.

blocks.text: Bring back your line drawing if it is here. Find a line choice you tried. If the drawing is elsewhere, you can start a simple shape on fresh paper today. The new work will still show how you take part.
Today you use tone. Tone means how light or dark an area looks. With one pencil, you can make pale grey, dark grey and shades between them. The white paper can be a light area too.
This continues the same arts activity: drawing. You are adding another way to use the tool. You will keep a result and explain what you learnt from making it.
Put your paper on a firm surface. Test the pencil in the practice space. Ask for a different grip or tool if you cannot use it with comfort.

stages.title: Starter · create the need
stages.data-ta1: Create A, B and C as described and check visibility. Offer the examples close up if projection washes out the pale tone. Accept pointing or ordered letter cards.

blocks.text: Look at the three boxes marked A, B and C. A is white paper. B is pale grey. C is darker grey. The boxes are the same size, so look at the tone rather than their shape.
Point to the darkest box. Now find the lightest. Where would you put B between them? You can show the order with the letters instead of saying it aloud.
Tone can help separate one area from another. When a dark shape sits beside a light area, its edge may be easier to see. When their tones are close, the edge may blend in.
Neither effect is always best. A maker might want a clear sign or a soft shape. Think about which effect could help the small drawing you want to make.

stages.title: I Do · model
stages.data-ta1: Model the strokes and pauses live. Avoid equating a darker result with superior work. Keep a visible white area so tone comparison is based on the actual marks.

blocks.text: I make a small tone patch with light strokes. I hold the pencil at a comfortable angle. I move back and forth across the patch without digging the point into the page.
After the first layer, I lift the pencil and look. Some paper shows between the marks. I add another light layer where I want a darker tone. A darker area does not need a painful grip or a torn page.
I leave a small area white beside the patch. That gives me a light tone to compare it with. Now I add more layers to the other side. I can see a change from white through grey to dark.

blocks.title: Build tone in gentle layers
blocks.caption: Pause between layers to see what the pencil does.
blocks.alt: Four linked boxes: start lightly, look beside white paper, layer to darken an area, and choose the tone to keep.

blocks.text: I stop when the tone suits my purpose. More layers are not always better. If I want a pale cloud, making it very dark may change the effect I wanted.
My model learning note says: light layers let me choose when to stop. I point at the pale and dark ends to show what I mean.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits
stages.data-ta1: Keep all four statements on view and collect every pupil’s response before giving the key. Read or point through the model without supplying the pupil’s reason.

data.heading: Choose what changes tone
data.instruction: Sort each action. Does it change light and dark, or does it change something else?

items.label: Leave a patch of paper white.
items.feedback: White paper can keep a light area in the drawing.

items.label: Use a sheet that is twice as wide.
items.feedback: This changes the size of the sheet. It does not itself make a mark lighter or darker.

items.label: Add a gentle pencil layer over a patch.
items.feedback: A further pencil layer can darken the patch. Check what your own tool does.

items.label: Turn the paper so your arm has room.
items.feedback: This changes your reach. It can help you work, but is not itself a tone change.

data.discussion: Try a pale patch and a dark patch. Point to what you did to make each one. If they look alike, say so and check the action you used.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect
stages.data-ta1: Make wider-gap and closer-gap patches with the same pencil. Demonstrate the second crossing set accurately if naming cross-hatching. Keep all models visible for the lab.

blocks.text: There is another way to make tone. I draw a set of short lines that run alongside each other. This is hatching. I leave gaps so the light paper shows through.
When I put similar lines closer together, less white shows between them. The area often looks darker. I try it on a spare patch before using it in the drawing.

blocks.title: Line spacing changes the tone
blocks.caption: Compare the real patches before choosing a spacing.
blocks.alt: Two columns compare wider gaps showing more paper with closer lines showing less paper.

blocks.text: I can add a second set across the first. That is cross-hatching. Both sets remain visible and cross each other. It is a different action from tracing one line again and again.
I do not need to use every method in one drawing. I choose layers or hatching for the effect I want. My learning can name the method and what I noticed it did.
A neat patch is not the only useful result. A rough patch can show a rough surface. Describe what the marks suggest instead of calling all rough marks wrong.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab
stages.data-ta1: Give time for actual patches before checking them. Prompt a description of the pupil’s action and observation; do not insist that every trial must show a successful difference.

blocks.text: Create your own practice patches now. Make a pale patch and a darker one. Use gentle layers, or try changing the gaps between hatch lines. Keep your hand comfortable.
Pause and compare the patches you have just made. Which action gave you a tone you can use? Point to that action’s result while you explain it to a partner or an adult.
The checker asks: what did you do here? You might say that you added a layer or left wider gaps. If the patches look alike, check what actually changed before you claim a difference.
Keep the practice on your sheet. Add a short note about something you found. You may speak your note for a scribe. They read it back so you can check the meaning.

stages.title: Independent · evidence
stages.data-ta1: A supplied outline may support access, but pupils must make their own tone choices and marks. Keep time for making and a short located learning account; never write a pupil’s conclusion for them.

blocks.text: Make a small drawing that uses tone. You can redraw a simple shape from last time or choose a fresh shape. Decide where you want a light area and where a darker area could help.
Use layers or hatch lines to build the tone. Look up from the page between stages. If two areas merge when you wanted a clear edge, try a different tone on spare paper first.

Choose a result to keep. Point to an area where the technique did something you noticed. Say what you tried and what you learnt. Include a line choice from the earlier lesson if it helps explain the drawing activity.

items: Core: use a large simple outline and the pale/dark prompts. Make your own tone marks. Point and explain a learning point for a verbatim scribe.
Extend: choose and apply a tone method, keep the drawing and record your own learning about the action and result.
Challenge: keep the same participation and learning evidence, then compare layers with hatching in two small areas.

blocks.text: Your account need not say you improved by a set amount. Explore asks what you learnt through taking part. A note about what you would try differently can be honest and useful.

stages.title: Exit · name the activity
stages.data-ta1: Check the activity label and file-plus-location. Do not count line and tone as the two required arts activities, and do not record a second activity before it has happened.

blocks.text: Find your chosen drawing and learning note. Does the note describe something you really tried? Can you point to the part that helped you learn it?
Put the line and tone records together under drawing, activity one. They are two lessons within one arts activity. The next activity will use folded paper to make forms that stand.

Append the work to the Explore-A file. Give its actual name plus page or slide. For spoken learning, give the sound file and timecode. Ask the adult to check that the work and your words can both be found.
Keep one idea you want to remember from drawing. You may also leave a question about a mark that did not behave as you expected.

print.intro: Try a tone method, make your own drawing and keep a learning point about the action and result. Line and tone belong to the same drawing activity.

checks: I made tone marks myself using an accessible tool.
